passage: Zubin, your fest committee is blaming the treasurer for the rain-out? Let your Afreen khala tell you something. When I was twenty, our college drama club held an open-air play in August. A storm came, the stage flooded, and we lost all the ticket money. At the review, everyone turned on Farooq, who had chosen the venue. "It was obvious it would rain!" I was scared to speak, but I asked, "What did we know in June when he booked it? The forecast said clear, the hall was double the price, and all of us voted yes." The room went quiet. Farooq looked at me as if I'd thrown him a rope. We ended up writing a rain plan for next time instead of a list of blame.

qa.q: What did the forecast say in June when Farooq booked the venue?
qa.a: The forecast said clear.

qa.q: Why did the club members feel sure it was obvious it would rain?
qa.a: The club members felt angry and certain because they already knew about the storm, so the risk looked obvious looking back. They forgot how the choice had looked in June.

qa.q: What could Zubin's fest committee take from this story?
qa.a: They could ask what was known when the treasurer made each choice, and turn the review into a plan for next time rather than a search for someone to blame.

qa.q: How might Farooq have felt when Afreen asked her question?
qa.a: Farooq likely felt relieved and less alone, as though someone had thrown him a rope while the whole room blamed him.

grounding: Shows a young club member reviewing a failed event fairly by asking what was actually known when the venue was chosen.

passage: The college debating society had fifteen minutes in a stuffy classroom, fans dead because of a power cut, to review last week's disaster. Their inter-college debate had drawn eleven people. "It was obvious nobody would come on a Friday before exams," someone snapped. Eyes turned to Keerthana, who had picked the date. She stared at her notes. Ayesha, the secretary, fanned herself with the attendance sheet and said, "Wait. When we chose the date, did anyone know the exam timetable?" Silence. "It came out two days after we booked the hall," she went on. "So what should we check next time before fixing a date?" In the heat, the list came quickly: exam calendar, other colleges' fests, a backup date.

qa.q: How many people did the inter-college debate draw?
qa.a: The debate drew eleven people.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana stare at her notes when eyes turned to her?
qa.a: She probably felt blamed and embarrassed, since the room was treating her choice of date as an obvious mistake.

qa.q: What made Ayesha's question useful even with only fifteen minutes?
qa.a: Asking what was known when the date was chosen showed the timetable came out later, which quickly turned blame into a practical checklist for next time.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt as the room turned on Keerthana?
qa.a: Ayesha may have felt uneasy that the blame was unfair, which is why she asked whether anyone had known the exam timetable when the date was chosen.

grounding: Shows a student reviewer asking what was known when a failed event's date was chosen, instead of calling the risk obvious afterwards.

passage: In a crowded café near the university in Pune, the entrepreneurship cell met to review their failed startup expo. Three sponsors had pulled out a week before, and the stalls stood half empty. "Pradeep should've known the big sponsor was shaky," one member said. "It was obvious." Pradeep, the coordinator, looked down at his cold coffee. Siddharth pulled out his phone and scrolled back through the planning group. "Look. On the day Pradeep signed them, they'd confirmed in writing and paid half. Did anyone here raise a doubt back then?" Nobody had. "So the choice was reasonable with what we knew," Siddharth said. "What we missed was a backup sponsor. Let's fix that."

qa.q: What had the sponsor done on the day Pradeep signed them?
qa.a: They had confirmed in writing and paid half.

qa.q: Why does it feel obvious to the member that Pradeep should have known?
qa.a: The member feels frustrated about the failed expo, and knowing that the sponsor pulled out makes the risk seem clear. So the member judges the past choice by today's result.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do that a fair reviewer should do?
qa.a: He checked the planning messages to see what was known at the time, confirmed nobody had doubted it then, and turned the talk to a real gap: a backup sponsor.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep during the review?
qa.a: Pradeep sits quietly over his cold coffee, likely feeling blamed and embarrassed until the planning messages show his choice made sense at the time.

grounding: Shows a team calling a failed event's risk obvious and a fair reviewer checking what was actually known when the choice was made.

passage:
"So the biryani stall flopped," said Arif bhai, pouring tea. "Obviously. Who sells biryani at a fest in April heat? Everyone wanted cold drinks."
"Totally obvious," agreed Nazia, his wife, "and it was right next to the gate. Too much dust."
Shreya, twenty and still sore, put down her cup. "Wait. When we chose biryani in February, what did we know?"
"That it'd be hot?"
"The fest was supposed to be in the evening. They moved it to two p.m. three days before. And last year's biryani stall sold out."
Nazia paused. "Okay. And the gate spot?"
"That was the only spot left after the committee reshuffled. We didn't choose it."
Arif bhai scratched his beard. "Hmm. So it wasn't a stupid plan."
"It was a reasonable plan with bad luck," said Shreya. "Next time we'll ask what happens if the timing changes."

qa.q: What time did the fest get moved to?
qa.a: They moved it to two p.m. three days before.

qa.q: Why did the failure seem "obvious" to Arif bhai and Nazia?
qa.a: They felt confident judging the stall by what they know now, the heat and the dusty gate, without thinking about what Shreya's team knew in February.

qa.q: Which question from Shreya changed the review, and why?
qa.a: "When we chose biryani in February, what did we know?" It moved the talk from blame to the facts available then, like the evening timing and last year's sell-out.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt hearing her family call the plan obviously wrong?
qa.a: She was already sore about the loss, so the easy blame probably stung, which is why she stopped to set the record straight.

grounding: At home, relatives call a failed fest stall obviously doomed, and a young woman asks what was actually known when the choice was made.

passage: Last monsoon our college trekking club cancelled a Sahyadri trek halfway because of a landslide warning, and twenty-two people had to be brought back in jeeps at extra cost. I'm Harish, the club secretary, and I sat in the review meeting the week after. Everyone went after Ojas, who had planned it. "Trekking in July? It was obviously risky." "He should have known." Ojas just stared at the table. I didn't think it was fair, but I didn't want a shouting match. So I pulled up the planning chat from June and read it out. The forecast then: light rain. The forest office had said the trail was open. Three other colleges had booked the same route. Then I asked, "Knowing only this, what would we have decided?" The room went quiet. Someone said, "Probably the same." We agreed next time to add a clear turn-back rule, not a scapegoat.

qa.q: How many people had to be brought back in jeeps?
qa.a: Twenty-two people.

qa.q: Why did the club members feel sure the trek was "obviously risky"?
qa.a: They knew the landslide warning had come and felt frustrated about the extra jeep costs, so July trekking looked reckless in hindsight. They forgot that the forecast and the forest office had said it was fine at the time.

qa.q: What did Harish choose to do instead of arguing, and why did it work?
qa.a: Harish read out the June planning chat and asked what they would have decided knowing only that. Seeing the old information made the blame fade.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt while everyone blamed him?
qa.a: Ojas probably felt ashamed and alone, staring at the table, and may have been relieved when Harish showed the plan had been reasonable.

grounding: A club secretary sees a review blame the trek planner and brings back what was known then, turning blame into a fair lesson.
